entries.description: A sheet of cells that is printed, shown or exported — the thing every printed form is built into. Two are normally in play at once: a TEMPLATE, opened by name and never written to, and an OUTPUT document, empty at the start, that areas of the template are put into one after another. Nothing is drawn until an area is put.

Opens a template held in Common templates and answers with it as a SpreadsheetDocument. Raises when there is no such template — the name is checked at run time, not at compile time. A metaobject's own template is reached instead through its manager: Documents.GoodsIssue.GetTemplate("Waybill").
entries.parameters: name — the template's name in Common templates.
entries.return_descr: SpreadsheetDocument — the template. Take a fresh one for each document of a batch: putting areas can change the template's own column widths.

entries.description: Takes a COPY of a named area of the template, to be filled in and put. Because it is a copy, the same area can be taken again for the next row with the previous row's values gone. A named area is either a band of rows or a block of columns; naming both at once with a vertical bar — "TableHeader|Amount" — takes their intersection, which is how one row of a table is assembled out of column blocks.
entries.parameters: label — the area's name as declared on the template. "row|column" takes the intersection.
entries.return_descr: SpreadsheetDocument — the copy, ready to fill.

entries.description: Adds an area BELOW what is already there, starting a new line. The first block of every row is put; everything after it on the same row is joined. `groupLevel` places the rows in a collapsible group, which is what a report's levels are drawn with.
entries.parameters:
table — an area taken with GetArea, or a whole document.
groupLevel — outline level for the rows added; 0 for none.

entries.description: Adds an area TO THE RIGHT of what was last put, on the same line. This is the second of the two directions a blank is built in, and it is what makes an optional column possible: a row is put as its first block and joined with only the column blocks this document needs. A column block left out does not leave a gap — give its width to a neighbour, or the table prints narrower than its own frame.
entries.parameters:
table — an area taken with GetArea.
groupLevel — outline level for the columns added; 0 for none.

entries.description: The template's fillable holes, by name. A cell only takes a value through this if it was declared as a PARAMETER or a TEMPLATE cell — a cell left as plain text ignores what is assigned and prints its own text, which is how a form comes out blank with no error anywhere. Assignment is by name: `Parameters.<name> = value`, or Set(name, value) when the name is computed; Get(name) reads one back and Count() says how many names the cells declare. Fill(source) copies a Structure's or a row's fields into the parameters of the same names — but only as many of them, from the first, as the area declares parameters, so a wider source loses its later fields; set those one by one.
entries.parameters: Count(), Get(name), Set(name, value) and Fill(source) — see SpreadsheetParameterCollection.

entries.description: The named ROW areas of the template, by name — each answering with a SpreadsheetAreaRange: its Label and the first and last row it covers (Start, End, counted from 0). It says WHERE an area lies; it is not the area, and nothing in it can be changed. Column blocks are not listed — they are reached through GetArea("Row|Column") — and taking an area to fill is GetArea's job too. A sheet made with New has no areas.
entries.example:
Header = Template.Areas.Header;
Message(Header.Label + ": rows " + String(Header.Start) + "-" + String(Header.End));

entries.description: ONE CELL, by number, to be read or changed in place — the only way into a cell the template does not name. What comes back carries the whole of what a cell is: Value, Font, AlignHorizontal and AlignVertical, TextColour and BackgroundColour, TextOrient, BorderLeft / BorderRight / BorderTop / BorderBottom, Size (how many cells it is merged across) and ReadOnly. All of them read; all but AlignHorizontal, AlignVertical and TextOrient also write — an assignment to those three raises in this build. A named area is better wherever there is one — a name survives rows being inserted above it and a number does not.
entries.parameters: row, col — the cell's position, COUNTED FROM ZERO. The editor's margin and the designer's tools show the same cell as row 1, column 1, so a number copied from there addresses the NEXT one. Area(0, 0) is the top-left cell.
entries.return_descr: The cell — a SpreadsheetArea. A sheet has no edge: a cell past what is filled in reads empty and takes what is written into it. A negative row or column raises.

entries.description:
A band of whole rows as a SpreadsheetDocument OF ITS OWN — not a reference into this one. Use it to lift a part of a sheet out: it can be put into another document, shown or printed by itself. To change a single cell in place, use Area.

Only the rows can be given: the member takes two arguments, so the column bounds its body would read cannot be passed — Range(0, 1, 0, 1) raises "too many parameters".
entries.parameters: rowStart, rowEnd — the rows, inclusive, counted from 0. An end past the content is the content's own end.
entries.return_descr: SpreadsheetDocument — the part, as a document.

entries.description: Opens the finished sheet in a window for the person to read, page through and print for themselves. This is the ordinary end of a printing routine — printing straight to the printer is a preference, not a second command.
entries.parameters: title — the window's caption; name the document, not the template.

entries.description:
Sends the sheet straight to a printer, without a dialog: to PrinterName, or to the system default when that is empty. Printing needs a window — on the server, in a background or a scheduled job, it raises ("the server has no forms").

The member takes no argument: the showPrintDlg its own hint names is not accepted, and Print(False) raises "too many parameters".

Which printer this sheet goes to when it is printed without a dialog. Empty means the system default. Set it on the sheet rather than asking a person each time when the destination is a fact about the document — labels to the label printer, invoices to the office one.

Which language the TEMPLATE is read in. Set it on the template once, before any area is taken, and every translated caption inside it switches; only the strings the routine builds itself have to be handled separately. A blank for a foreign counterparty is this one assignment, not a second template.

Ends the page here, so what follows starts on a new sheet of paper. Put one between documents when several are printed into one sheet — without it the second invoice starts halfway down the first one's page. PutVerticalPageBreak does the same across the width.
Ends the page across the width, so the columns that follow go on the next sheet. A wide report needs this where a table has more columns than the paper can carry.

Opens a collapsible group of rows; EndRowGroup closes it. Groups nest, and that is how a report's levels are drawn — one pair per level entered. BeginColGroup / EndColGroup do the same across the columns. Rows put with a non-zero groupLevel are placed into a group without these being called.
Closes the group of rows opened by BeginRowGroup. Every Begin needs its End: a group left open swallows everything put after it, including the totals.

How many rows stay in view while the rest scrolls — the table's heading, normally. FixedLeft does the same for columns. This is about reading on screen; the printed page repeats nothing on its own account.
Empties the sheet of everything put into it. Use it when one document object is reused for a second report rather than making a fresh one; a template is never cleared, it is simply not written to.

How many columns stay in view while the rest scrolls sideways — the row headings, normally. FixedTop does the same for rows; 0 fixes none. Like FixedTop it is about reading on screen: the printed page repeats nothing on its own account.

Whether the person can type into the sheet once it is shown. False — the default for a new document — leaves it editable; True shows it for reading only. One cell of an editable sheet is locked with the cell's own ReadOnly: `Sheet.Area(row, col).ReadOnly = True`.

Opens a collapsible group of columns; EndColGroup closes it. The column twin of BeginRowGroup: groups nest, one pair per level, and areas joined with a non-zero groupLevel are placed in a group without these being called.
Closes the group of columns opened by BeginColGroup. Every Begin needs its End: a group left open takes in every column joined after it.

One cell of a sheet, by number — what Area(row, col) answers. It is a window onto the cell, not a copy: what is written into it goes into the document it came from, at once. Never made with New. It carries the cell's text (Value) and its look: Font, TextColour, BackgroundColour, AlignHorizontal, AlignVertical, TextOrient, the four borders, Size (how far it is merged) and ReadOnly.

Rows and columns count from 0, and a sheet has no edge: a cell past what is filled in reads empty and takes what is written into it.
The cell's fill, as a Colour. Assigning anything but a Colour raises.
The colour of the cell's text, as a Colour. Assigning anything but a Colour raises.
entries.example: Sheet.Area(5, 2).TextColour = New Colour(192, 0, 0);   // a negative balance in red

entries.description: Which way the cell's text runs — a member of SpreadsheetOrient, Horizontal by default. ⚠ It reads; an assignment raises in this build ("does not support this operation"): the setter does not take the enumeration's own members. A template cell keeps the orientation it was drawn with.
The cell's font, as a Font. Assigning anything but a Font raises. Taking the font of a cell that already has the wanted one is the shortest way to repeat it.
entries.example: Sheet.Area(1, 0).Font = Sheet.Area(0, 0).Font;   // the heading's font on the next row

entries.description: Where the text stands across the cell — a member of SpreadsheetHorizontalAlignment, Left by default. ⚠ It reads; an assignment raises in this build ("does not support this operation"): the setter does not take the enumeration's own members. A template cell keeps the alignment it was drawn with.

Where the text stands between the cell's top and bottom — a member of SpreadsheetVerticalAlignment, Top by default. ⚠ It reads; an assignment raises in this build ("does not support this operation"): the setter does not take the enumeration's own members.

The cell's left border, as a SpreadsheetBorderRow — its Style, Colour and Width. Assigning one sets the border. A border's own fields take no value, so a border is copied from a cell that has the wanted one, or removed with `New SpreadsheetBorderRow()` (style None). BorderRight, BorderTop and BorderBottom are the other three sides.
The cell's right border, as a SpreadsheetBorderRow. Read and assigned as BorderLeft is: copied from a cell that has the wanted one, or removed with `New SpreadsheetBorderRow()`.
The cell's top border, as a SpreadsheetBorderRow. Read and assigned as BorderLeft is: copied from a cell that has the wanted one, or removed with `New SpreadsheetBorderRow()`.
entries.example: Cell.BorderTop = Sheet.Area(0, 0).BorderBottom;   // the heading's rule above this cell

entries.description: The cell's bottom border, as a SpreadsheetBorderRow. Read and assigned as BorderLeft is: copied from a cell that has the wanted one, or removed with `New SpreadsheetBorderRow()`.

How far the cell is merged, as a Size — 1 x 1 for a cell of its own. ⚠ The two names are crossed: Width is the number of ROWS the cell spans and Height the number of COLUMNS. Assigning `New Size(1, 3)` merges the cell with the two to its right; the cells it covers stop being cells of their own, for the grid and for printing alike.
entries.return_descr: Size — Width the rows, Height the columns.
entries.example:
Title = Sheet.Area(0, 0);
Title.Size = New Size(1, 5);   // one row, five columns

entries.description: Whether the person may type into this one cell when the sheet is shown editable. False by default. The whole sheet is locked with the document's own ReadOnly.

The cell's text. Reading answers what the cell SHOWS, always as a String: on an output document, an area's parameters as they were filled in; on a template, what is written in the cell — a parameter cell's NAME, not a value. Writing stores the value's text: 12.5 is kept as "12.5". A cell past what is filled in reads "".
entries.example:
Sheet.Area(2, 3).Value = 12.5;
Message(Sheet.Area(2, 3).Value);   // "12.5" - text, not a number

entries.description: What a sheet's Areas answers: the named ROW areas of the template, as a read-only Structure — the key is the area's name, the value its SpreadsheetAreaRange. It is read the way a Structure is: `Areas.Header`, Get(name), Property(name, found), Count(), and For Each gives a KeyValue per area. Insert, Delete and Clear are not there. Column blocks are not in it; they are reached through GetArea("Row|Column"). A sheet made with New has no areas, and Count() answers 0.
How many named row areas the template has.
The SpreadsheetAreaRange of the area with this name, or Undefined when the template has none — asked without raising, where `Areas.<name>` raises on a name that is not there.
Whether the template has an area of this name; when it has, its SpreadsheetAreaRange is put into the second argument.
entries.parameters:
name — the area's name.
valueFound — a variable that receives the area's SpreadsheetAreaRange.

entries.description: Where a named row area of a template lies: its Label and the first and last row it covers. An element of the template's Areas. It describes the area, it is not the area: its three fields are read only — an assignment to them is dropped without a word — and taking the area to fill is GetArea's job.
The area's name, as the template declares it — the name GetArea takes.
The area's first row, counted from 0 as Area and Range count rows.
The area's last row, counted from 0 and belonging to the area.

What a sheet's Parameters answers: the parameters its cells declare, each a property by its own name — `Area.Parameters.Number = Ref.Number`. A cell takes a value this way only when the template declares it a Parameter cell, or a Template cell with [names] in its text (SpreadsheetTemplate); a plain Text cell prints what is written in it, whatever is assigned.

Get and Set reach any name, also one no cell declares: a value set under such a name is kept with the sheet but shows nowhere, which is how a misspelt name fails silently. Count() counts only the names the cells declare.

How many parameter names the sheet's cells declare: each Parameter cell's name, each [name] inside a Template cell, and each cell's details parameter. A name given only through Set is not counted, so a sheet made with New answers 0.
The value held under a name, or Undefined when nothing is. The name need not be declared by any cell. On a composed report the value under a cell's details parameter is a SpreadsheetDetails.
Holds a value under a name — what assigning the property does, but with the name as a string, so it can be computed. The name need not be declared by any cell; one that is not shows nowhere.
entries.parameters:
name — the parameter's name.
value — what the cells declaring it show.

entries.description: Copies a source's properties — a Structure's keys, a row's fields — into the parameters of the same names. ⚠ It reads only as many of the source's properties, from the first, as the area declares parameters: a source with more fields than that loses those past the count, even when they match a parameter. Keep the source to the area's own names, or set the rest one by one.
entries.parameters: source — a value with properties: a Structure, a table's row.

entries.description:
One border of a cell: its Style (a SpreadsheetBorder), Colour and Width. A cell's BorderLeft, BorderRight, BorderTop and BorderBottom answer with one and take one.

New makes "no border" — style None, black, width 1 — and nothing else: arguments given to New are ignored, and the three fields read but take no value (an assignment is dropped without a word). So a border is set by copying it from a cell that has the wanted one, and removed with a new one.
The line the border is drawn with — a member of SpreadsheetBorder; None when there is no border. Read only.
The border's colour, as a Colour; black for a new one. Read only.
The line's width; 1 for a new one. Read only.

What a cell of a COMPOSED report is bound to: the value it shows, plus the field it is a reading of and what kind of field that is. The composer makes one per cell, under the cell's details parameter, as it writes the sheet; nothing else makes one, and there is no New.

Outside its three properties it IS the value it wraps — its text, its number, its comparisons — so a template prints it as it always printed the value, and comparing it with a plain value compares the two values. Opening it opens the value; a figure with no card of its own opens the nearest heading above it that has one.
The PATH of the field the value is a reading of, as the composition groups and filters by it — `Goods.Group`, not the column's title. Read only.
What kind of field that is — a member of SpreadsheetFieldKind: a Dimension the report grouped by, a Resource it measured, or a plain Field. Read only.
The value itself, unwrapped — a reference, a number, a date. Read only.
Which way a cell's text runs. A cell's TextOrient answers with a member, written SpreadsheetOrient.<Name>.
Along the row. The default.
Turned on its side — for a heading over a narrow column.
Where a cell's text stands across the cell. A cell's AlignHorizontal answers with a member, written SpreadsheetHorizontalAlignment.<Name>.
At the cell's left edge. The default.
In the middle of the cell — a title, a heading over several columns.
At the cell's right edge — where figures go, so their digits line up.
Where a cell's text stands between its top and bottom. A cell's AlignVertical answers with a member, written SpreadsheetVerticalAlignment.<Name>.
At the top of the cell. The default.
Halfway between the top and the bottom — text beside a taller neighbour.
At the bottom of the cell.
The line a cell's border is drawn with — a SpreadsheetBorderRow's Style, written SpreadsheetBorder.<Name>.
No line: the border is not drawn. What a new SpreadsheetBorderRow has.
A solid line — a table's ordinary rule.
A dotted line.
A line of short dashes.
A dash-and-dot line: dashes with a dot between each two.
A line of long dashes.

How a template cell's text that is wider than the cell is laid out — the cell's Fit mode in the template editor. A script meets it nowhere yet: no member of a sheet or of a cell reads or takes it. Its members are named so that a value can be written and compared.
The text runs on over the empty cells to its right. The default.
The text is cut off at the cell's edge.
The text breaks onto further lines inside the cell.

What a template cell holds — its Fill type in the template editor. It decides whether Parameters reaches the cell: a Parameter cell and a Template cell are filled, a Text cell is printed as written. A script meets it nowhere yet: no member of a cell reads or takes it; it is set in the template.
Plain text, printed as written: nothing assigned to Parameters reaches it. The default — and the reason a form comes out blank when a cell meant to be filled was left as text.
The cell holds a parameter's NAME and prints the value Parameters holds under it.
Text with [names] inside, each replaced with the value Parameters holds under it — "Invoice No. [Number] of [Date]".

What kind of field a cell of a composed report is a reading of — a SpreadsheetDetails's Kind, written SpreadsheetFieldKind.<Name>. A Dimension is part of the context of every figure under it; a Resource is the figure itself.
A field shown as it is — neither grouped by nor measured: a column of a detail record.
A field the report grouped by: a heading's value, part of the context of every figure under it — what a detail is filtered by.
A measured figure — a sum, a total. The figure itself, never part of anybody's context.
